items.title: Linus Pauling worked out how molecules hold together
items.claim: In 1939 Linus Pauling published The Nature of the Chemical Bond, integrating quantum mechanics, electronegativity, hybridisation and resonance into a single framework. It defined how chemists have thought about bonding ever since.

options.text: Quantum-mechanical superposition (resonance) of multiple valence-bond structures, plus a numerical scale of electronegativity that quantified how unevenly atoms share electrons

items.reveal:
Pauling's electronegativity scale (1932) assigns each element a number measuring how strongly it attracts shared electrons. Differences in electronegativity predict bond polarity and whether a bond is more covalent or more ionic.

His valence-bond theory described molecules with resonance structures — quantum superpositions of multiple Lewis structures. Benzene's two equivalent Kekulé structures, the carbonate ion's three equivalent resonance forms, and the carboxylate's symmetric pair all came from this framework.

Pauling won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He won a second Nobel — the Peace Prize 1962 — for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. Only Marie Curie and Pauling have won Nobels in different categories.
items.why: Chemistry today still uses Pauling's electronegativity, hybridisation and resonance vocabulary. His book defined how to talk about bonds.

items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.

items.title: An atom is about 99.9999999999999 percent empty space
items.claim: If a hydrogen atom were scaled up so the nucleus was the size of a marble (1 cm), the electron would orbit roughly 1 kilometre away. Almost everything 'solid' around you is overwhelmingly empty.
items.prompt: If atoms are mostly empty, why does a wall feel solid?

options.text: Walls have very few atoms in them
Solidity comes from electromagnetic repulsion between electron clouds and from Pauli exclusion preventing electron states from overlapping — not from particles physically touching
Atoms swell up to fill space when forces are applied
The 'empty space' is filled with a dense medium

items.reveal:
A hydrogen atom is about 10 to the minus 10 m across. Its nucleus is about 10 to the minus 15 m. The ratio is 100,000 — so atoms are about 10 to the 15 times more volume than nuclei.

When you touch a table, no atoms touch. Electromagnetic forces between the electron clouds of your fingertip and the wood push back. The Pauli exclusion principle prevents the electrons from sharing identical quantum states, contributing the actual 'incompressibility' of matter.

Rutherford's 1909 gold foil experiment showed this directly — most alphas passed through gold foil unscathed because gold atoms are mostly empty.
items.why: Students treat atoms as small spheres of stuff. They are tiny dense nuclei surrounded by enormous shells of probability.
